title: Query evaluation: processing models
lead: Iterator interfaces, operator state, pipelining, vectorisation and materialisation.

sections.title: Iterator interface and control flow
sections.html:
Iterator contract and demand flow

A processing model specifies when operators run and in what unit they exchange data. Iterator/Volcano operators expose open,next,close and retain per-instance state between calls. open initialises; next returns one tuple or EOF; close releases resources. The same contract lets a filter consume either a scan or another join.

root.open()
try:
  while (tuple = root.next()) != EOF:
    deliver(tuple)
finally:
  root.close()

Calling the root causes demand to travel down the plan, while results travel up. LIMIT can stop demand after enough outputs, but cannot remove work already required by a blocking child. Cleanup is needed even on early termination or failure.

PDF pp. 1–5

sections.title: Stateful operator implementations
sections.html:
Selection, heap cursor and resumable nested loops

selection.next():
  repeat:
    r = child.next()
    if r == EOF: return EOF
    if predicate(r): return r
heapScan.next():
  while page exists:
    if a live slot remains:
      r = record at cursor; advance slot cursor; return r
    advance page cursor; reset slot cursor
  return EOF
nestedLoop.next():
  while currentOuter != EOF:
    while (s = inner.next()) != EOF:
      if predicate(currentOuter,s): return (currentOuter,s)
    inner.close(); inner.open()
    currentOuter = outer.next()
  return EOF

Selection may consume several child tuples to produce one output. The scan must skip empty/deleted positions and remember its page/slot; returning a tuple must not reset it. A nested-loop operator retains the current outer tuple while its inner cursor resumes after a match. Its open initialises both children and the first outer tuple; close closes both.

PDF pp. 6–8

Blocking sort and the source hash-plan call order

The two-pass sort’s open consumes the child into sorted runs, then prepares one input buffer per final run. Its next chooses the smallest current tuple, advances that run and refills pages as needed. close deletes temporary runs. More than B−1 final runs requires additional passes before this merge.

For the source projection-over-hash-join plan, demand begins at projection, reaches join, consumes the R scan to build, then requests S through value>100 selection and probes R. Projection runs for each emitted pair. The numbered arrows show control transfer, not a statement that all operators produce output before building is complete.

PDF pp. 9–11

sections.title: Pipelining and vectorisation
sections.html:
Pipeline boundaries and per-tuple overhead

A streaming filter/projection can pass one result onward before consuming all input. Sort blocks on its input; hash join blocks on its build side but can stream its probe side. Grouping or DISTINCT on unsorted data may need retained state or a blocking implementation.

Iterator composition is simple, but each tuple crosses several next-call boundaries. Virtual calls, branches, code locality and resume-state bookkeeping become significant for in-memory data. A common interface guarantees composability, not optimal CPU throughput or full pipelining of every plan.

PDF pp. 12–13

Vector batches and their final partial output

A vectorised next returns a batch. Selection processes an input batch in a tight loop, writes qualifying positions/tuples to an output batch and emits when capacity is reached. At EOF it must also emit a nonempty partial batch; otherwise the final results are lost.

Calls and state updates are amortised across tuples and SIMD can process several values together. A hash join still builds before probing; batching does not remove algorithmic dependencies. Batch size balances cache locality, call overhead and memory use, making this model particularly useful for analytical scans.

PDF pp. 14–15

sections.title: Materialisation model
sections.html:
Materialisation and the three-model comparison

ModelControlTransfer unitTypical fit
IteratorTop-down pullOne tupleGeneral purpose
VectorisedTop-down pullBatchOLAP
MaterialisedBottom-upWhole intermediateSmall OLTP intermediates

In the source materialised plan, scan R and S, produce the selected S relation, build/probe the join and then project its result. An operator finishes its collection before the parent consumes it. Small collections can improve locality; large collections require memory or temporary disk writes. These workload labels are tendencies, not guarantees. The physical join/sort algorithm and memory budget still determine its detailed behaviour.

PDF pp. 16–18

quiz.question: Can one Filter.next() call invoke child.next() more than once?
options: Yes, to discard tuples that do not satisfy the predicate
No, it always calls the child exactly once
Only when the child is an index
quiz.explanation: The filter continues reading input until it finds a qualifying tuple or reaches EOF.

source.summary: The full official PDF has been reviewed. Coverage includes the open/next/close iterator interface and composability; selection, heap-scan, and nested-loop state; blocking sorts and hash builds; pipelining, LIMIT, and iterator overhead; vectorized batch and SIMD processing; and materialization, execution direction, and workload trade-offs. The explanations and calculations are original teaching material rather than reproductions of the slides.
